texts.preamble: Manoj Kumar Sahu vs The State Of Madhya Pradesh on 13 October, 2025 Author: Milind Ramesh Phadke Bench: Milind Ramesh Phadke Neutral Citation No. 2025:Mphc-Gwl:25780 1 In The High Court Of Madhya Pradesh At Gwalior Before Hon'Ble Shri Justice Milind Ramesh Phadke On The 13th Of October, 2025 Misc. Criminal Case No. 3504 of 2022 Manoj Kumar Sahu Versus The State Of Madhya Pradesh And Others Appearance: Shri Sanjay Kumar Bahirani - Advocate for the applica Shri Samar Ghuraiya - Public Prosecutor for the State Order
texts.facts: The present application under Section 482 of Cr.P.C is filed for quashment of criminal proceedings pending before the Judicial Magistrate First Class Chachoda, District Guna in RCT No.991 of 2021 arising out of FIR bearing Crime No.50/2021 registered at Police Station Kumbhraj, District Guna for the offence punishable under Sections 420, 272 and 273 of IPC against the applicant. As per prosecutor story, the informant, Mr. Naveen Jain, Food Safety Officer, Guna, appeared at the police station and submitted a typed letter to the Deputy Controller and Reporting Officer (Integrated Inspection Form), and the District Food & Drug Administration Officer, Guna, M.P., to the effect that the accused, coriander trader Manoj Sahu, son of Mr. Shivcharan Sahu, resident of Kumbhraj, was adulterating coriander and committing fraud, which falls under Sections 272, 273, and 420 of the IPC. NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2025:MPHC-GWL:25780 2 MCRC-3504-2022 The Deputy Controller and Reporting Officer, Food & Drug Administration, District Guna, M.P., under reference No. Ghadya/2021/147, Guna, dated 16.02.2021, addressed to the Station House Officer, Police Station Kumbhraj, District Guna (M.P.), requested registration of an FIR against the accused, Manoj Sahu, son of Mr. Shivcharan Sahu. Manoj Kumar Sahu vs The State Of Madhya Pradesh on 13 October, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/101302693/ 1 Regarding the above, it is stated that on 23.01.2021, under the directions of the SDM, Chachoda, the Food Safety Officer, Mr. Naveen Jain, visited Police Station Kumbhraj. During inspection at the police station premises, a truck with registration No.HP 12 H9611 was checked. The truck was found carrying 400 bags of coriander intended for human consumption. The coriander belonged to trader Manoj Sahu, son of Shivcharan Sahu, from the firm "Shri Manoj Kumar & Company," Galla Mandi, Kumbhraj. The truck was en route to deliver the coriander to M/s. Agrahari Masala Udyog, Phulwari, Amethi (Uttar Pradesh). In the presence of the Tehsildar, under his guidance, samples of the coriander (whole and split mix, loose) were collected with the consent of the seller, based on suspicion of adulteration. These samples were sent for testing to the State Food Testing Laboratory, Bhopal, in accordance with the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006. The laboratory report (Ref. FTL/KKS/R2650, dated 08.02.2021) declared the coriander sample as substandard. It appeared that the sale of substandard coriander for human consumption was fraudulent. Following the verbal instructions given by the Collector, Guna, in a time-bound meeting, and in compliance with the Madhya Pradesh NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2025:MPHC-GWL:25780 3 MCRC-3504-2022 Government, Ministry of Public Health and Family Welfare, letter No.03/Food/2/59/2020/4858, Bhopal, dated 09.11.2020, point No.14, the Food & Drug Administration Officer requested that an FIR be registered against the applicant. Learned counsel for the applicant submits that the applicant has always procured and sold coriander from verified and lawful sources, maintaining proper records of purchase, sale, and dispatch. The FIR is based solely on a laboratory report of a sample taken from a truck consignment. The sample collection, sealing, and dispatch were not conducted strictly in accordance with the procedure prescribed under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 and the Food Safety and Standards (Food Products Standards and Food Additives) Regulations, 2011. The goods in question do not fall within the ingredients of Sections 272 or 273 IPC, as there was no intention to sell adulterated food knowingly or to cause injury to health.
texts.arguments: It is further submitted that the applicant denies any fraudulent intent or inducement and no act of deception or dishonest inducement was committed. The supply of coriander was made in good faith, for lawful commercial purposes, and with intention to provide wholesome food. In the absence of mens rea, Section 420 IPC is not attracted. It is further submitted that the coriander consignment does not constitute unsafe or substandard food as defined under Sections 3(zx) of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006. Section 3(zx) defines "unsafe food" as an article of food which is likely to cause injury to health, and Section 3(x) defines "sub-standard food" as food which does not conform to the standards NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2025:MPHC-GWL:25780 4 MCRC-3504-2022 set under the Act. The consignment supplied meets all applicable standards, and any variation in laboratory test results cannot automatically render the food unsafe or substandard, particularly when proper handling, storage, and sampling Manoj Kumar Sahu vs The State Of Madhya Pradesh on 13 October, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/101302693/ 2 procedures may not have been strictly followed. The applicant is ready to provide all purchase invoices, supply records, and storage logs to verify compliance. It is also submitted that Section 31(1) of the FSS Act prescribes strict procedures for sampling and analysis, and any deviation from these procedures renders the conclusions of the report unreliable. The Hon'ble High Courts of Punjay & Haryana and Bombay in cases such as Anil Kumar vs. State of Haryana [(2014) 1 ILR (P&H) 186] and M/s Marico Ltd. vs. Food Safety Officer [2020 (81) PTC 244 (Bom)] have held that mere minor non-conformity in food quality, without proof of injury or fraudulent intent, does not constitute an offence under IPC or the FSS Act. Per contra, the learned Public Prosecutor for the State has opposed the prayer and submitted that the FIR in question is based on prima facie material and is fully maintainable. 3 Further, as per Section 3(zx) of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, which defines "sub-standard," any article of food shall be deemed sub- standard if it does not meet the specified standards, but not so as to render the article of food unsafe, which goes to imply that even if a food article is found to be sub-standard, it would not necessarily be unsafe for consumption. Mere allegation of substandard food, without specific evidence of adulteration intended to defraud or cause harm, does not prima facie constitute an offence under the IPC. The commercial scale of the consignment or lawful procurement does not transform ordinary business activity into a criminal offense, particularly where no injury to health or deceptive intent is established. For reference, Sections 272, 273 and 420 of IPC are quoted hereinbelow: Section 272 - Adulteration of food or drink intended for sale Whoever adulterates any food or drink, so as to render it noxious, shall be punished with imprisonment of either NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2025:MPHC-GWL:25780 7 MCRC-3504-2022 description for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine which may extend to one thousand rupees, or with both. Section 273 - Sale of noxious food or drink Whoever sells or exposes for sale, or has in his possession for the purpose of sale, any adulterated food or drink, knowing or having reason to believe it to be adulterated, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine which may extend to one thousand rupees, or with both. Section 420 - Cheating and dishonestly inducing delivery of property Whoever cheats and thereby dishonestly induces any person to deliver any property to any person, or to consent that any person shall retain any property, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine. In exercising its inherent powers under Section 482 CrPC, the Court is guided by the principles laid down in State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal [1992 Supp (1) SCC 335], wherein the Apex Court has held that an FIR may be [LEAKAGE_MASK] if the allegations, even if taken at face value, do not prima facie constitute an offense, or if the continuation of the investigation amounts to NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2025:MPHC-GWL:25780 8 MCRC-3504-2022 abuse of the legal process. The Court is also guided by Suresh Chand Jain v. Union of India [AIR 2001 SC 571] and subsequent judgments emphasizing the need to prevent harassment and oppression by unfounded prosecutions.
